candidateRows: The logical problem of evil fails because neither omnipotence nor perfect goodness entails the hidden premises needed to make God and evil contradictory.
This extended argument directly contests the alleged logical incompatibility at the heart of the motion and supplies both free-will and morally sufficient-reason defenses.
The traditional atheist claim that an omnipotent, perfectly good God cannot logically coexist with evil.

Craig reconstructs the logical objection, identifies two unstated assumptions, disputes each, and argues that a possible proposition combining divine existence with permitted evil establishes consistency.
Humans cannot reliably infer that God probably lacks sufficient reasons for evil because their temporal perspective and causal knowledge are severely limited.
This is Craig's first principal answer to the probabilistic problem of evil, challenging the epistemic inference from apparently pointless suffering to divine improbability.
The probabilistic objection that apparently gratuitous evils make the existence of God unlikely.

Craig shifts from logical consistency to probability and argues that finite observers cannot survey providential history, remote consequences, or the reasons relevant to divine permission of suffering.
Distinctive Christian doctrines make evil less surprising because life's purpose is knowledge of God, suffering may serve that end, and eternal recompense changes its significance.
The move supplies a positive theistic framework under which suffering is compatible with divine purposes, rather than relying solely on human ignorance of those purposes.
The assumption that a loving God's primary purpose would be maximizing happiness during earthly life.
Craig contrasts happiness-centered expectations with Christian claims about knowing God, entry into an eternal kingdom, and an afterlife whose fulfillment can outweigh severe temporal suffering.
Even if evil lowers the probability of God, rational judgment must consider the full body of evidence, which Craig contends can still make God's existence probable.
This move states Craig's ultimate comparative-evidence answer and supports his concluding claim that neither form of the problem of evil justifies atheism.
The inference from the existence and scale of evil alone to the overall improbability of God's existence.

Craig argues that probabilities depend on background information, invokes other purported evidence for God, and concludes that evil should not be evaluated in isolation from the total evidential case.
The tsunami raises a religious-pluralism problem because its victims held many faiths, while Christian exclusivism appears to deny salvation to many who suffered and died.
The argument connects the debate's signature disaster to competing religious claims and complicates the suggestion that suffering serves a common salvific or greater-good purpose.
Craig's appeal to divine purposes, knowledge of God, and eternal salvation as context for earthly suffering.
Grayling notes that the disaster killed adherents of diverse religions and no religion, then questions how a proposed greater good relates to incompatible faiths and exclusivist salvation claims.
If an intelligent supernatural agent is interested in humanity, the world's tsunamis and childhood cancers initially indicate that it is either malevolent or less than omnipotent.
The inference from observed suffering to the character or power of a putative deity is Grayling's direct negative answer to whether the relevant form of theistic belief is reasonable.
Craig's conclusion that belief in God remains rational despite natural evil and severe human suffering.

Grayling conditionally grants a supernatural, active, intelligent, and interested agent, then asks what the observed world implies about it and presents deficient goodness or power as the initial alternatives.
Craig's defenses create a dilemma: either God lacks the power to prevent suffering in a free world, or God can prevent it but permits it for a proposed greater good.
This dilemma targets the internal relationship between Craig's free-will defense and greater-good defense, pressing whether they preserve both omnipotence and benevolence together.
Craig's claims that free will limits feasible creation and that benevolence may permit suffering for sufficient reasons.

Grayling reconstructs Craig's two answers, criticizes cognitive limitation as an unrestricted appeal to mystery, and argues that inability and deliberate permission yield conflicting accounts of divine responsibility.
Ordinary standards of loving fatherhood make it implausible that a benevolent agent would subject conscious creatures to extreme suffering merely for an unseen greater good.
The analogy supplies Grayling's substantive moral objection to the greater-good defense by testing divine benevolence against recognizable standards of protective care.
Craig's contention that a perfectly good God may permit terrible suffering to secure morally sufficient overriding ends.

Grayling grounds expectations about an intelligent, interested deity in human relationships and argues that a caring parent would not impose catastrophic suffering on children for benefits they cannot perceive.
An omnipotent God should be able to create free creatures in a world with far less suffering, so the claimed necessity of this world's natural evil requires unsupported modal assumptions.
The move directly attacks the necessity premise behind the free-will and greater-good defenses and extends responsibility across intertwined natural and moral evils.
Craig's claim that God may be unable to actualize a sufficiently good free world containing less evil.

Grayling proposes worlds with free agency but little or no physical suffering, questions why this quantity of evil is required for good, and argues that divine willing of natural evil implicates related human agency.
The character of the actual world makes belief in an almighty and all-loving deity unreasonable, especially when supernatural agency already rests on multiple speculative assumptions.
The passage consolidates Grayling's cumulative case and gives his direct answer to the debate question concerning an omnipotent, benevolent deity and the observed world.
Craig's overall defense of the reasonableness of belief in an omnipotent and perfectly loving God despite evil.

Grayling reviews the speculative path to an interested supernatural being, contrasts world-denying and worldly conceptions of value, emphasizes sentient welfare, and closes by rejecting the reasonableness of the traditional deity.
Possible morally sufficient reasons for permitting suffering defeat the claimed logical incompatibility between God and evil.
This move directly contests a necessary premise of the logical problem of evil and assigns its proof burden to the atheist.
Grayling's claim that a powerful and benevolent deity would not permit terrible suffering.
Craig distinguishes divine obligations from those of a human father, invokes possible overriding reasons, and argues that logical incompatibility remains unproved.
Human cognitive limitations prevent justified probability judgments that God lacks sufficient reasons for observed evil.
The argument attacks the evidential inference from apparently gratuitous suffering to God's improbability by challenging human epistemic competence.
The secular inference that the world's observed suffering makes a concerned deity unreasonable or improbable.
Craig lists limits on human knowledge and uses chaos theory and a branching-life illustration to argue that distant consequences cannot reliably be assessed.
Christian theism makes evil less improbable because suffering may help bring people freely into God's kingdom and eternal life.
This supplies an affirmative theistic explanation for why natural and moral evil could coexist with a divine salvific purpose.
The argument that natural and moral evils make the existence of the Christian God improbable.
Craig says God's primary purpose is knowledge of himself rather than earthly happiness and treats suffering as a possible means toward freely accepted salvation.
Theological qualifications repeatedly move the concept of God away from the familiar caring-father model used to motivate belief.
The move challenges the conceptual stability of the theistic defense and argues that its qualifications undermine ordinary grounds for understanding divine goodness.
Craig's rejection of the human-father analogy and his qualified account of divine power and moral responsibility.
Grayling argues that attempts to reason from a loving creator continually encounter revised divine attributes, leaving the proposed moral relationship obscure.
The distinction between a logically possible world and one feasible for God is insufficiently explained, especially regarding free creatures without natural evil.
This attacks the mechanism by which the free-will defense seeks to deny that God could actualize a better world containing free agents.
Craig's claim that logically possible worlds containing free agents and less evil may nevertheless be infeasible for God.
Grayling accepts a distinction between possibility and desirability but says he cannot see the asserted difference between logical possibility and divine feasibility.
Appealing to unknown morally sufficient reasons for tsunamis and childhood cancer does not make belief in a caring powerful deity reasonable.
The move directly addresses the debate's governing question by arguing that unexplained possible goods cannot reconcile traditional divine attributes with the actual world.
Craig's appeal to unknown morally sufficient divine reasons for permitting terrible pain and suffering.
Grayling argues that merely trusting that drowning or painful cancer serves an unknown good leaves an incoherence between a concerned powerful being and this world.
Neither expert abandonment of the logical problem nor appeals to human ignorance and Christian doctrine adequately answer the probabilistic problem of evil.
This consolidated reply rejects Craig's authority appeal, skeptical-theist reasoning, and Christian framing as support for the coexistence of God and evil.
Craig's claims about philosophical consensus, cognitive limits, Christian doctrine, and the total evidential case.
Grayling says authority does not refute an argument, ignorance cannot supply unknown justifying goods, and the Gospel portrait of God conflicts with natural evil.
Ordinary moral knowledge remains reliable enough to assess suffering despite uncertainty about remote consequences and chaotic causal effects.
The argument resists skeptical theism by defending the human capacity to make sufficiently dependable moral judgments about harms and benefits.
Craig's contention that unpredictable long-term consequences prevent justified judgments about apparently gratuitous evil.
Grayling contrasts giving ice cream with kicking an ankle and argues that practical moral understanding is rich enough to bear on the reasonableness question.
The harsh facts of the world make belief in even a minimally aware and influential supernatural being unreasonable on the total evidence.
This is Grayling's culminating application of the world's suffering to the motion, extending the objection from traditional theism to a minimal deity.
Craig's claim that Christian salvation and future fulfillment reconcile divine goodness with suffering in this life.
Grayling contrasts pastoral assurances with sophisticated qualifications, characterizes future compensation as a blank check, and concludes that the total evidence diminishes reasonableness.
A world containing free individuals but no natural evil appears logically possible, so the theist must explain why it would be infeasible for God.
The challenge targets a crucial gap between logical possibility and divine feasibility in extending the free-will defense to natural rather than moral evil.
Craig's insistence that classical omnipotence excludes only contradictions and that some possible worlds are not feasible.
Grayling sets aside verbal contradictions such as round squares and asks for a substantive reason why free creatures could not inhabit a world without natural evil.
The reality of evil supports God's existence because objective moral values would not exist without God.
This reverses the objection from evil into an affirmative argument for God and supplies a central foundation for the theistic case.
The objection that innocent suffering and natural evil count strongly against a just and loving God.
After a question about infants killed by a tsunami, Craig places evil alongside other evidence and develops a moral argument from objective evil to God's existence.
Objective facts about human needs, interests, sentience, and suffering can ground moral obligations without invoking God.
This directly contests the indispensable premise of Craig's moral argument by offering a secular basis for objective moral judgment.
Craig's claim that objective moral values cannot exist unless God exists.
Grayling argues that observable facts about human nature impose obligations and that moral understanding can mature historically while remaining responsive to objective conditions.
Human needs produced by evolution cannot furnish objective morality because other evolved creatures could possess radically different values.
The move defends the moral argument's disputed first premise by challenging the objectivity of Grayling's naturalistic moral foundation.
Grayling's proposal that natural facts about human needs and suffering objectively ground moral obligations.
Craig uses evolutionary contingency and an imagined extraterrestrial morality to argue that species-relative human attitudes do not constitute objective moral truths.
Natural facts about suffering constrain moral choice and provide a strong basis for mutual respect and kindness.
This preserves the secular grounding of morality under direct attack and explains how factual circumstances can constrain appropriate conduct.
Craig's argument that evolved human characteristics yield only species-relative attitudes rather than objective obligations.
Grayling points to changing moral judgments and then argues that pain, need, and other natural human facts make helping preferable to harming.
Without an objective transcendent standard, historical differences can be described as moral change but not genuine moral progress.
This attacks the evaluative force of the secular account by arguing that it cannot justify condemning past practices as objectively worse.
Grayling's claim that evolving responses to human needs amount to genuine moral progress on a naturalistic basis.
Craig argues that atheism permits comparison of changing social attitudes but supplies no objective measure for progress, blame, or moral truth.
A tsunami has a physical tectonic explanation and is morally indifferent in itself, though its human consequences are tragic.
The move directly addresses the debate's defining natural-evil example without assigning the disaster a divine purpose or moral agency.
The theistic framing of the tsunami as an event whose occurrence or permission requires a morally sufficient divine explanation.
Answering an audience question, Grayling separates the tectonic cause of the tsunami from the tragedy of its consequences and notes the resulting human support.
Natural disasters may fit God's plan because an omniscient God can order complex contingencies toward bringing people freely into relationship with him.
This supplies Craig's principal response to apparently gratuitous natural evil by appealing to morally sufficient reasons and providential complexity.
The challenge that no adequate divine reason explains why a devastating tsunami and comparable suffering were permitted.
Craig denies that humans can identify the tsunami's precise purpose but argues that divine middle knowledge can coordinate remote contingencies while preserving creaturely freedom.
God may be unable to create significantly free moral agents with comparable moral good while guaranteeing that they never choose evil.
The argument supplies the logical core of the free-will defense by distinguishing an evil-free animal world from significant moral agency.
The audience challenge asking whether God could have created a world containing no moral evil.
Craig says God could create an evil-free world without higher agents, but making significantly free agents choose only good would be logically impossible.
Neither the logical nor probabilistic problem of evil defeats Christian theism, and Christian purposes make evil unsurprising if God exists.
This closing synthesis directly addresses the motion by combining logical compatibility, epistemic limits, divine purposes, and positive evidence for God.
Grayling's cumulative contention that the world's suffering makes belief in a powerful and benevolent God unreasonable.
Craig's summation claims compatibility between God and evil, rejects confident probability judgments about divine reasons, and invokes life's eternal purpose and other theistic arguments.
Religious faith may sustain people psychologically, but selective claims to divine knowledge and mystery reveal a nonrational basis.
This closing reply targets the reasonableness of theism itself by distinguishing faith's psychological usefulness from rational evidential warrant.
Craig's closing appeal to Christian consolation, Christ's suffering, divine love, and human inability to discern God's reasons for evil.
Grayling grants that Mabel's faith was sustaining but argues that believers inconsistently claim knowledge of God's love while invoking cognitive limits about suffering.
Proportioning belief to evidence supports a secular humanist morality grounded in shared human experience, sympathy, and concern for others without requiring religion.
This supplies the secular alternative to faith-based moral reasoning and directly supports the con side's account of how ethical concern can remain rational and substantive without God.
Craig's presentation of religious faith as an uplifting and adequate foundation for moral conviction and conduct.

After criticizing faith for accommodating apparent inconsistencies, Grayling contrasts it with evidence-proportioned secular humanism and grounds fellowship and morality in common human needs and experience.
Concern motivated directly by empathy for another person's suffering is more worthy of respect than similar conduct motivated by ideological or religious commitment.
The comparison reinforces the secular account of moral motivation by arguing that fellow feeling can provide a purer basis for humane conduct than religious or ideological incentives.
The earlier theistic suggestion that religious faith provides a compelling source of moral uplift, commitment, and action.
Grayling closes his secular moral argument with a comparison between empathy-driven assistance and assistance prompted by doctrine, faith, or anticipated moral credit.
